primer.text: From Speed you already know how to average distance over time for steady motion. This lesson turns that arithmetic into a picture: the distance-time graph, where the steepness of every straight line is a speed and every flat stretch is a rest. It is the first graph-reading skill the motion topic builds on.

lessons.title: What a distance-time graph shows
sourceHeadings: Constant speed on a distance-time graph
lessons.opening: A distance-time graph is a picture of a journey: how far the object sits from its starting point at every moment of the trip. This lesson trains the two readings that unlock every such graph — what the steepness tells you, and what a flat line tells you.
keyPoints: A distance-time graph plots how far an object is from its starting point against time.
A straight line means constant speed; the steeper the line, the larger the speed.
A flat horizontal line means the object is stationary.
A curve means the speed is changing — steepening is speeding up, flattening is slowing down.

low.restatement: On a distance-time graph the distance from the start runs up the side and time runs along the bottom. Straight lines are constant speeds, flat lines are rests, and curves are changing speeds.
low.analogy: Think of the line as a hill-walk profile tipped on its side: the steeper the path climbs, the faster you are walking; where it levels out, you have stopped for a break.
low.examPointer: Questions usually ask what a section of line shows — answer with the motion word (stationary, constant speed, speeding up, slowing down), not with a description of the line's shape.

medium.restatement: Because the vertical axis is distance, the gradient at any point equals the speed there. A straight line has one gradient throughout, so straight means constant speed; a changing gradient means a changing speed.
medium.analogy: Treat each point of the line like a car's speedometer needle frozen at that instant: straight lines hold the same reading, curves swing it up or down.
medium.examPointer: Compare-the-two-lines questions are graded on gradient: the steeper line is the faster object, even if it ends lower — never rank speeds by final height.

check.stem: On a distance-time graph, a section of the line is completely flat and horizontal. What does this show?

options.text: The object is moving at a large constant speed
options.explanation: A large constant speed is a steep straight line, not a flat one.

options.text: The object is stationary
options.explanation: Distance from the start is not changing, so the object is not moving.

options.text: The object is accelerating steadily
options.explanation: Acceleration needs a curve; a flat line has no steepness to change.

options.text: The object is returning to its starting point
options.explanation: Returning means distance decreasing — a downward-sloping line.

check.stem: Two objects each trace a straight line on the same distance-time axes. Line P is steeper than line Q. What follows?

options.text: P has travelled further in total
options.explanation: Total distance comes from where the line ends, not from its steepness.

options.text: P is accelerating
options.explanation: Straight lines carry one unchanging gradient, so neither object accelerates.

options.text: P is moving faster than Q
options.explanation: On distance-time axes the gradient is the speed, and P's gradient is larger.

options.text: Q is stationary
options.explanation: A stationary object gives a flat line, not a sloped one.

check.stem: How is the speed of an object read from a straight line on a distance-time graph?

options.text: From how high the line finishes
options.explanation: The finishing height is the total distance, not the speed.

options.text: From the steepness of the line — steeper means faster
options.explanation: The gradient of a distance-time line is the speed.

options.text: From the physical length of the drawn line
options.explanation: Drawing size is a page artefact and carries no motion information.

options.text: Straight lines carry no speed information
options.explanation: A straight line is exactly the case where one speed value applies throughout.

check.stem: A distance-time graph shows a smooth curve instead of a straight line. What does the curve indicate?

options.text: The speed is changing
options.explanation: A curve's gradient changes from point to point, so the speed changes too.

options.text: The object is stationary
options.explanation: Stationary objects give flat lines, not curves.

options.text: The graph has been plotted incorrectly
options.explanation: Curves are the correct picture for changing speed, not a plotting mistake.

options.text: The object moves at constant speed
options.explanation: Constant speed demands a constant gradient, which a curve does not have.

check.stem: Where on a distance-time graph do you read the total distance an object has travelled?

options.text: At the steepest gradient of the line
options.explanation: The steepest gradient reads the largest speed, not the distance covered.

options.text: At the final height of the line
options.explanation: The vertical value at the end of the line is the distance reached from the start.

options.text: In the area under the line
options.explanation: Area under a line is a velocity-time reading; distance-time graphs are read by height.

options.text: On the time axis
options.explanation: The time axis shows when things happened, not how far.

check.stem: State what a flat, horizontal line on a distance-time graph tells you about the object's motion.
check.modelAnswer: The object is stationary (at rest, still) — its distance from the starting point is not changing, so it has stopped moving and its speed is zero.

check.stem: State what the steepness of a straight line on a distance-time graph represents.
check.modelAnswer: The speed — the steepness (gradient) of the line: the steeper the line, the larger the speed it represents.

check.stem: Explain why two objects drawing straight lines of different steepness are both moving at constant speed.
check.modelAnswer: A straight line has the same gradient — the same slope — at every point, and on a distance-time graph that gradient is the speed. Because neither line's gradient changes (stays unchanging), both speeds stay constant — only their values differ.

check.stem: Object X's line on a distance-time graph is noticeably steeper than object Y's over the same interval of time. State which object moves faster and how the graph shows it.
check.modelAnswer: X moves faster: over the same time interval X's line rises further, so X's gradient — and therefore its speed — is larger.

lessons.title: Changing speed and the gradient
sourceHeadings: Changing speed on a distance-time graph
Calculating speed from a distance-time graph
lessons.opening: When speed changes, the distance-time line stops being straight. This lesson turns the line's steepness into a number — the gradient — and uses it to calculate speeds from graph axes, including the unit conversions examiners expect.
keyPoints: Speed is the gradient of a distance-time line: change in distance divided by change in time.
Convert axis units to metres and seconds before reading a gradient, giving a speed in m/s.
A large gradient triangle gives a more accurate gradient than a small one.
A line sloping back toward zero distance shows the object returning to its start.
A downward slope marks the direction of travel, not deceleration — speed is the gradient's magnitude.

low.restatement: The gradient of the line — how much the distance changes for each bit of time — is the speed. Draw a large triangle on the line, divide the distance change by the time change, and convert the units first.
low.analogy: A gradient triangle is like a ladder leaned against the line: the taller and wider the ladder, the more reliable your read of how steep the hill really is.
low.examPointer: Show the unit conversions explicitly — kilometres to metres and minutes to seconds — because the marks sit in the conversion as often as the division.

medium.restatement: Gradient equals change in vertical over change in horizontal, so on distance-time axes it is distance change over time change in the axis units. Steepening curves mark acceleration; flattening curves mark deceleration; a falling line is a return journey whose speed is the magnitude of its gradient.
medium.analogy: Read a curve like a ramp into a car park: the entry steepens as you speed up, flattens as you brake, and the downward exit ramp still has a speed even though it heads back to the ground floor.
medium.examPointer: Large gradient triangles earn method marks; tiny triangles squeezed against the line lose accuracy and credit. Quote the final speed to 2 or 3 significant figures.

check.stem: The gradient of a distance-time line is the speed. Which pair of quantities gives that gradient?

options.text: Change in time divided by change in distance
options.explanation: That inverts the axes and yields s/m, not m/s.

options.text: Change in speed divided by change in time
options.explanation: That is the acceleration formula from velocity-time work, not a distance-time reading.

options.text: Change in distance divided by change in time
options.explanation: Vertical change over horizontal change on these axes is distance over time = speed.

options.text: Distance multiplied by time
options.explanation: Multiplying the axes quantities has no motion meaning here.

check.stem: A graph's axes read distance in km and time in minutes, and a gradient triangle spans 8 km over 6 minutes. The speed in m/s is closest to:

options.explanation: 8 divided by 6 gives km per minute; reading that as m/s skips both conversions.
8000 divided by 60 converts only the minutes; the 360 s total needs minutes times 60.
Converting the distance but never dividing by the time is not a speed.

check.stem: Why should a large gradient triangle be drawn when reading a gradient from a graph line?

options.text: It makes the finished graph look fuller
options.explanation: Presentation is not the reason; the triangle size changes the accuracy of the reading.

options.text: It avoids having to convert units
options.explanation: Unit conversion is still required whatever the triangle size.

options.text: Small triangles are banned in exams
options.explanation: Small triangles cost accuracy, not legality — the guidance is about reliability.

options.text: The same reading uncertainty becomes a smaller fraction, so the gradient is more accurate
options.explanation: Larger spans dilute the fixed reading error, giving a gradient closer to the true value.

check.stem: A line on a distance-time graph slopes downward, back toward zero distance. What is happening?

options.text: The object must be decelerating
options.explanation: The speed is the gradient's magnitude; a straight downward line is constant speed toward the start.

options.text: The object is returning toward its starting point
options.explanation: Distance from the start is decreasing, so the object is heading back the way it came.

options.text: Time is running backwards
options.explanation: Time still advances left to right; only the distance value falls.

options.text: The graph has been plotted wrongly
options.explanation: Distance can decrease on a return journey; a falling line is perfectly valid.

check.stem: What are the SI units of the gradient of a distance-time graph?

options.text: metres per second (m/s)
options.explanation: Metres on the vertical axis divided by seconds on the horizontal axis gives m/s.

options.text: seconds per metre (s/m)
options.explanation: That inverts the axes.

options.text: metres (m)
options.explanation: Metres alone is the vertical axis quantity, not its gradient.

options.text: metres per second squared (m/s squared)
options.explanation: That is acceleration, which belongs to velocity-time graphs.

check.stem: State the equation used to find speed from a distance-time graph.
check.modelAnswer: speed = gradient = change in distance divided by change in time (the rise-over-run of the graph line).

check.stem: Recall the SI units distance and time should be converted to before reading a speed from graph axes.
check.modelAnswer: Distance in metres and time in seconds (the SI units), so the gradient comes out in metres per second (m/s).

check.stem: Explain why a large gradient triangle gives a more reliable speed than a small one.
check.modelAnswer: The gradient is the distance change divided by the time change. A larger triangle uses bigger changes, so the same small reading error is a smaller fraction of each value — the calculated gradient is more accurate, with less uncertainty, and sits closer to the true speed.

check.stem: A train's distance-time graph shows a straight line rising 8 km in 6 minutes. Calculate the speed in m/s, showing the unit conversions.
check.modelAnswer: 8 km = 8000 m and 6 min = 360 s, so speed = 8000 divided by 360 = 22.2 m/s (to 3 significant figures).

glossary.definition: A plot of how far an object is from its starting point against time taken.
The steepness of a line, worked out as the change in the vertical axis divided by the change in the horizontal axis.
Not moving at all — shown by a flat, horizontal line on a distance-time graph.
Speed that does not change, shown by a straight line on a distance-time graph.
Speeding up, shown on a distance-time graph by a line that steepens.
Slowing down, shown on a distance-time graph by a line that flattens.

workedExample.prompt: A distance-time graph is drawn below for part of a train journey. The train is travelling at a constant speed. Calculate the speed of the train.
steps: Draw a large gradient triangle on the graph and label the change in distance and the change in time using the units stated on each axis.
Convert to standard units: the distance travelled is 8 km = 8000 m, and the time taken is 6 mins = 360 s.
State that the gradient of a distance-time graph equals the speed: speed = gradient = change in distance / change in time.
workedExample.finalAnswer: 22.2 m/s (8000 m divided by 360 s = 22.2 m/s to 3 significant figures)
